content: Before taking chloroquine, inform your doctor or pharmacist about all medications you are currently using, including prescription drugs, over-the-counter medications, and herbal products. This is important because many drugs, including chloroquine, can affect heart rhythm, potentially leading to a condition known as QT prolongation. Certain vaccines, such as the rabies and cholera vaccines, may not be as effective if administered while you are taking chloroquine. If you suspect an overdose and experience severe symptoms like loss of consciousness or difficulty breathing, call emergency services immediately (911 in the U.S.). For non-emergency situations, contact a poison control center. U.S. residents can call 1-800-222-1222, and Canadian residents can call 1-844-764-7669. If you are taking chloroquine for an extended period, regular medical and laboratory tests are necessary. These may include eye exams, reflex tests, liver and kidney function tests, EKGs, and complete blood counts. Ensure you attend all scheduled medical and lab appointments. When traveling to areas where malaria is prevalent, use protective measures such as wearing appropriate clothing, applying insect repellent, and sleeping under bed nets. Stay indoors or in screened areas whenever possible. If you are using chloroquine to prevent or treat malaria, use it only for the specific travel or condition for which it was prescribed. If you miss a dose of chloroquine, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is close to the time of your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular dosing schedule. Do not double the dose to catch up. Store chloroquine at room temperature, away from light and moisture. Avoid storing it in the bathroom. Do not flush medications down the toilet or pour them into a drain unless instructed to do so. Properly discard this product when it is expired or no longer needed. Chloroquine is used to prevent or treat malaria caused by mosquito bites. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) provides updated guidelines and travel recommendations for malaria prevention and treatment worldwide. Chloroquine is not recommended for the treatment of COVID-19 unless you are enrolled in a clinical study. Take this medication orally, usually with food, to prevent stomach upset, and follow your doctor’s instructions precisely. The dosage and duration of treatment depend on your medical condition and response to therapy. To prevent malaria, take chloroquine as directed, typically once a week on the same day each week. Mark your calendar to help you remember. This medication is usually started 1 to 2 weeks before entering a malaria-endemic area. If you are also taking medications for diarrhea (e.g., kaolin) or antacids (e.g., magnesium/aluminum hydroxide), take chloroquine at least 4 hours before or after these products. Use this medication consistently to achieve the best results. Do not stop taking it without consulting your doctor, and continue taking it for the full prescribed duration. Inform your doctor if your condition persists or worsens. Note that chloroquine may not prevent malaria in all cases. If you develop fever or other symptoms of illness, seek medical attention immediately, especially while in a malaria-endemic area or within two months of returning from such an area. You may require a different medication. Avoid mosquito exposure as much as possible. Common side effects of chloroquine include nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, headache, and diarrhea. Remember that this medication has been prescribed because your doctor has determined that the benefits outweigh the risks of side effects. Chloroquine may cause low blood sugar (hypoglycemia). Notify your doctor immediately if you experience symptoms such as sudden sweating, shaking, hunger, blurred vision, dizziness, or tingling in your hands or feet. If you have diabetes, monitor your blood sugar levels regularly. This medication may cause serious eye or vision problems, especially with long-term use or high doses. Rarely, it can cause a severe allergic reaction. This is not a complete list of possible side effects. In the U.S., contact your doctor for medical advice about side effects. In Canada, consult your doctor for guidance. Before taking chloroquine, inform your doctor if you are allergic to it, hydroxychloroquine, or any other substances. This product may contain inactive ingredients that could cause allergic reactions or other issues. If you have diabetes, chloroquine may affect your blood sugar levels. Monitor your blood sugar as directed and share the results with your doctor. Notify your doctor immediately if you experience symptoms of low blood sugar. Chloroquine may increase your sensitivity to sunlight. Limit your time in the sun, avoid tanning booths and sunlamps, and use sunscreen and protective clothing when outdoors. This medication can cause QT prolongation, a condition that affects heart rhythm. The risk of QT prolongation may be higher if you have certain medical conditions or are taking other drugs that can cause QT prolongation. Low levels of potassium or magnesium in the blood can also increase this risk, which may be exacerbated by certain medications (e.g., diuretics) or conditions such as severe sweating, diarrhea, or vomiting. During pregnancy, chloroquine should only be used when clearly necessary. This drug passes into breast milk. Drug interactions may alter how your medications work or increase the risk of serious side effects. Keep a list of all the products you use, including prescription and non-prescription drugs and herbal products, and share it with your doctor and pharmacist. Many drugs, besides chloroquine, can affect heart rhythm (QT prolongation). Certain vaccines, such as the rabies and cholera vaccines, may not work as effectively if administered while taking chloroquine.
